631.title: Fate, providence, or chaos
631.hook: either fate, or providence, or confusion; in each case keep your own mind (Meditations 12.14)
631.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this three-way reflection during uncertain waits, choosing a response that holds whether events are fated, guided or random.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vast gulf: a short life set in endless time, and what death should find. Your line was what will I be.

You're waiting for news you can't control. The test result. The job decision. The storm track on the weather map. Underneath the waiting sits a bigger question nobody can settle for you: is any of this planned? Is someone watching over it? Or is it all just weather? In this entry, at least, Marcus doesn't claim to settle it. He writes down all three answers.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE NEWS.` → `PLANNED, WATCHED, OR WEATHER?` → `FATE, PROVIDENCE, OR CHAOS.`

segments.voice: First, three possibilities. Either there's a fixed necessity, an order that can't be broken, Marcus writes; or a providence that can be moved by prayer; or a confusion with no purpose and no one directing it. Second, an answer for each. If it's unbreakable necessity, why resist it? If it's a providence that listens, make yourself worthy of help from the divine. If it's chaos with no one in charge, be content that in such a storm you have within you a mind that can steer. Third, the storm. And if the storm carries you off, he says, let it carry off the flesh, the breath, everything else. It won't carry off the mind. Fourth, why three. Some readers hear in the three the rival answers of his own day: a world of fixed order, a providence that listens, a world of chance. Marcus doesn't settle that argument here, and he ranks no one. He does something more practical: he makes sure his answer works whichever is true. In each case the work is the same: keep your own mind steady. You don't have to decide the biggest question before you can steady yourself inside it.

Notice which one steadies you.

Your line: keep my mind. The storm can take a lot, but not that. Day six hundred thirty-one, done.

632.title: If not true, don't
632.hook: if it isn't right, don't do it; if it isn't true, don't say it (Meditations 12.17)
632.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often treat 12.17 as a daily check, pausing before an act or a word to ask whether it is right and whether it is true.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fate: fate, providence or chaos, keep your own mind steady either way. Your line was keep my mind.

"Love the haircut." "Running five minutes late," sent from the couch. "No, it's fine, really." Most small untruths in a day are soft, quick, and meant to keep things moving. Nobody keeps count. In the last book of his notebook, Marcus writes himself a rule short enough for a sticky note, with two halves: one about your hands, one about your mouth.
screen: `LOVE THE HAIRCUT.` → `RUNNING FIVE MINUTES LATE.` → `A RULE FOR HANDS AND MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: "If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it." First, the shape. It's not a lecture on honesty. It's a filter with two gates. Before an act: is it right? Before a word: is it true? If the answer is no, you don't need a long debate. You just don't. Second, the Greek. The word for true is alēthes, from the family of alētheia, truth. Truth runs all through the notebook. In book three Marcus put it among his four great goods, and in book nine he calls the deliberate lie a kind of impiety, a wrong against nature itself, which he says is also rightly called truth. A lie, even a small one, is a mind saying something it knows isn't so. Third, what the rule doesn't say. It doesn't say: say every true thing. Marcus elsewhere tells himself to be kind, to correct people gently, to keep quiet when quiet is better. Between the untrue word and the cruel true word, there's a third door: silence, or a smaller true thing. "I'm not sure about the haircut, but you look happy" is true. So is "I'm still on the couch, leaving now." Fourth, why it's at the end. To many readers, book twelve reads like a man packing for a trip, keeping what's light and what matters. A two-gate rule is the kind of thing you pack.

633.title: All is opinion
633.hook: everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power (Meditations 12.22)
633.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often practice separating what happened from the judgment they've added to it, describing the event plainly and then choosing how to read it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two gates: is it right, is it true. Your line was a smaller true thing.

A text arrives: "we need to talk." Nothing else. In the next four minutes, the mind can get you fired, dumped, and blamed for something you can't remember doing. Then the follow-up lands: "about the weekend plans." The words didn't change. The world didn't change. What changed was the story built around four words. For Marcus, that gap, between what happens and what we make of it, is where much of our trouble lives, and it's the one place we can reach.
screen: `"WE NEED TO TALK."` → `"ABOUT THE WEEKEND PLANS."` → `THE STORY CHANGED, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Way back in book two, Marcus wrote himself a short line. In George Long's translation: "Remember that all is opinion." In book twelve he comes back to it, more or less: take your opinion away whenever you choose, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you'll find calm water, everything still, a bay without waves. First, what opinion means here. The Greek word is hypolēpsis: an assumption, the judgment you add to a thing. Not the event, but the label. "This is a disaster." "She did that on purpose." Second, what Marcus doesn't mean. He isn't saying nothing is real, or that facts are just viewpoints. The text came. The weekend plans exist. What's opinion is the weight: harmful, insulting, ruined. Third, the opinion is yours. Events aren't in your power. Your reading of them is, at least a little, at least after a breath. That's the hopeful half. If the storm were out there, you'd have to wait for the weather. If much of it is in here, you can row toward the bay. Fourth, a neighbor. Marcus links the idea in book two to a Cynic named Monimus, who apparently said that everything is smoke, or vanity. Marcus takes the sharper edge off it: not that nothing matters, but that what we add to things can be taken away.

634.title: You forgot
634.hook: when troubled, you've forgotten that each person's mind shares in the divine (Meditations 12.26)
634.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often use 12.26 as a checklist when upset, running through Marcus's reminders, among them that every person's mind shares in the same reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was calm water: drop the label, find the bay. Your line was in my power.

You walk into the kitchen and stand there. Why did you come in? You knew a second ago. Marcus thought being upset is a lot like that: not that you never knew the truth, but that it slipped out of your hand on the way in. So in book twelve he writes himself a list, not of new ideas, but of things he already knew and kept forgetting the moment someone annoyed him.
screen: `WHY DID I COME IN HERE?` → `NOT NEW IDEAS. OLD ONES, DROPPED.` → `YOU FORGOT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 12.26 opens, in plain words: when you're troubled by something, you've forgotten. Then he lists what. First, the list. You've forgotten that all things happen by the nature of the whole. That another person's wrong is theirs, not yours. That what's happening now has happened before and will again. That you're kin to every human being, not by blood or seed but by sharing in mind. Even yesterday's line is there: everything is opinion. Second, the line at the center: each person's mind, he says, is a god, and has flowed from there. The Greek word for mind is nous. For the Stoics, a divine reason runs through the whole world, and every human mind is a piece of it, a spark from the same fire. Readers take this differently. Some hear something close to religious faith. Some hear a poetic way of saying every person can reason, and so deserves respect. Marcus himself sometimes isn't sure what runs the world, as we saw a few days ago. Third, why it's in a list about being troubled. If the person who cut you off in traffic carries the same spark you do, your anger is aimed at a relative, a cousin in reason. That doesn't excuse what they did. It changes who you think you're dealing with. Fourth, the comfort in the word forgot. You don't need to become someone new. You need to remember what you already knew, which is why Marcus kept writing it down.

635.title: A small share of time
635.hook: how small a share of endless time is given to each of us (Meditations 12.32)
635.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the view of endless time as a way of sorting a day, setting the small things down and choosing a few to do well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was you forgot: being troubled means dropping what you already knew. Your line was I forgot.

Open the photos on your phone and scroll back. A year. Five. The faces get younger, the haircuts get worse, and somewhere in there is a day that seemed like it would never end. A whole life under one thumb. Marcus had no camera roll. But near the end of his notebook, an emperor stops and measures a life, his own included, against all of time.
screen: `SCROLL BACK FIVE YEARS.` → `A WHOLE LIFE UNDER YOUR THUMB.` → `A SMALL SHARE.`

segments.voice: Meditations 12.32, in George Long's translation: "How small a part of the boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man?" He goes on: it's swallowed up in the eternal almost at once. Then he widens the lens: how small a part of all matter, of the soul of the whole, of the earth you creep on. First, the measuring. Marcus has done this all through the book: Asia and Europe as corners of the universe, the present as a point. Here he aims it at himself. An emperor, measured against endless time, holds a tiny slice. So does everybody else. Second, why this isn't gloom. The point of 12.32 isn't that your life is worthless. It's that your share is given. Long's word is assigned: handed out, like a ration. You didn't earn it and you can't extend it. Which makes the question not how much do I have, but what do I do with the share in my hand. Third, what he does with it. Right after the measuring, the passage turns: he tells himself to think nothing great except to act as his own nature leads, and to bear what the common nature brings. Small share, plain job. Fourth, the Tuesday version. A day is a small share of a small share. You can't fill it with everything. You can fill it with a few things done as yourself, well. That's not shrinking your life. It's fitting your hands to it.

636.title: Depart content
636.hook: Marcus ends: go gladly, for the one who dismisses you is gracious (Meditations 12.36)
636.howItsDone: Readers often treat the last passage of the Meditations as an evening practice, ending the day as a complete act rather than an unfinished one.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, measuring a life as a small share of time, given, not earned. Your line was a small share.

The last line of a book carries weight. Readers remember it. Writers sweat over it. Marcus wrote his notebook to himself, so we can't be sure he chose his last line. But the passage that stands at the end, as the book has come down to us, is about a stage, an actor, and a man in charge of the show who says: that's enough, you can go. It's about death, and it's surprisingly gentle.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF A BOOK.` → `AN ACTOR, A STAGE, "THAT'S ENOUGH."` → `THE LAST WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. In 12.36 Marcus pictures a comic actor whom the official in charge of the games dismisses from the stage. The actor protests: but I've only played three of the five acts. The answer comes back, in effect: in life, three acts can be the whole play. The one who put the drama together decides when it's complete, and the one who ends it does too. You were the cause of neither. Second, the line itself, in George Long's translation: "Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied." The Greek word Long renders satisfied is hileōs, which also means gracious, kindly, at peace. So you could hear it both ways: go at peace, because the one releasing you is at peace with you; go gladly, because you're being dismissed kindly, not thrown out. Third, who that one is. Earlier in the same passage, Marcus names it: not a tyrant or an unjust judge sends you off the stage, but nature, the same nature that brought you onto it. Elsewhere he also speaks of the whole, of God, of the gods. Some readers hear a personal God here; some hear nature itself, the order of things. The text leaves room for both. Fourth, why it's for the living. Every day ends before you've finished everything. Every job, every season, every conversation gets called before act five. Marcus's last word is practice for the small endings: leave the stage without clutching the curtain.

637.title: Marcus' blind spots
637.hook: Christians were persecuted in his reign, and he made his son Commodus heir: admiration and honesty together
637.howItsDone: Many modern readers of the Meditations read them alongside the history of Marcus's reign, including the persecution of Christians and the succession of Commodus.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was depart content, the actor leaving the stage at peace. Your line was go gladly. This week we finished book twelve: fate, two gates, opinion, forgetting, a small share, depart content.

We've just spent more than a hundred days inside one man's notebook. We've heard him talk himself out of anger, into kindness, toward death without fear. It's easy, after that long, to start treating him like a saint. But Marcus Aurelius was also a Roman emperor, with an emperor's power, for nineteen years. And two facts from his reign sit uneasily beside the notebook. The path doesn't skip them.
screen: `A HUNDRED DAYS IN HIS NOTEBOOK.` → `ALSO AN EMPEROR, NINETEEN YEARS.` → `TWO UNEASY FACTS.`

segments.voice: First, the Christians. During Marcus's reign, Christians were put to death in several places. Around the year 165 in Rome, the teacher Justin was tried and executed. The judge was the city prefect, Junius Rusticus, the same Rusticus whom Marcus thanks in book one for lending him the works of Epictetus. In 177, in Lyon in Gaul, a group of Christians were tortured and killed, a story preserved by the church historian Eusebius. Historians debate how much Marcus directed any of this. There was no single empire-wide order, and much was local. But it happened under his rule, and some cases reached him. The Meditations mention Christians once, briefly and coldly, and even that line may have been added by a later hand. Second, Commodus. For most of the century before Marcus, emperors had passed power to adopted heirs chosen for ability, partly because they had no surviving sons. Marcus had one, and made him co-emperor in 177. When Marcus died in 180, Commodus ruled for twelve years, and ancient historians remember those years as cruel and chaotic. Third, what to do with this. Not to throw the notebook away, and not to explain the facts away. The man who wrote about kinship with every human mind also governed an empire that killed people for their faith. Both are true. Fourth, why it matters for us. Every person we admire, a teacher, a parent, a hero, comes with blind spots. Learning from someone doesn't require pretending they had none.
screen: `JUSTIN AND LYON: DEATHS IN HIS REIGN.` · `COMMODUS, A SON AS HEIR.` · `DON'T DISCARD, DON'T EXCUSE.` · `EVERY HERO HAS BLIND SPOTS.` · then, large: `BOTH AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you admire, living or dead, and let yourself feel what you admire in them; then, gently, let one real failing come into view too. Notice the urge to push one of them away, and try not to: hold both at once, like two stones in your hands.
Commodus. The son Marcus made co-emperor, remembered by ancient historians as cruel and chaotic once he ruled alone. Today's word.
Your line: both at once. Admiration and honesty can share one pair of hands. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Marcus wrote so beautifully. Was he a good emperor all the way through?
options: The notebook is wise, but Christians were killed under his rule and he chose Commodus.
